planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated leaf cuttings or divisions in spring in wet to saturated, acidic, nutrient-poor peat or sand in full sun; Chapman's butterwort grows in shallow standing water of Florida panhandle and Gulf Coast flatwoods bogs, tolerating wetter conditions than most butterworts.

directions: Plant nursery-propagated leaf cuttings or divisions in wet to saturated, acidic, nutrient-poor peat or sand in full sun. Chapman's butterwort forms a flat, ground-hugging rosette of pale yellow-green, sticky leaves that press directly against the soil surface, an adaptation to the shallow standing water of the wet Florida panhandle and Alabama flatwoods bogs where it grows, often with the rosette partly submerged during the wettest months. Striking violet-pink flowers on slender stalks appear in spring, held well above the low foliage, and the sticky leaf surface traps and digests small insects the same as other butterworts. It tolerates wetter, more consistently saturated conditions than most Pinguicula species, making it a good match for the lowest, wettest spot in a home bog garden alongside pitcher plants. Grow in pure rain water or distilled water and never fertilize, since both tap water minerals and ordinary garden fertility are fatal to butterworts over time.
sources: Carnivorous Plants of the Southeast (Larry Mellichamp)

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated leaf cuttings or divisions in spring in wet, acidic, nutrient-poor sandy or peaty soil in full sun to partial shade; blue butterwort is one of the most common and easily grown native butterworts of Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain pine savannas.

directions: Plant nursery-propagated leaf cuttings or divisions in wet, acidic, nutrient-poor sandy or peaty soil in full sun to partial shade. Blue butterwort forms a low rosette of pale green, sticky-glandular leaves that trap small insects, and in spring sends up striking, pale blue-violet flowers with a darker throat on wiry stalks well above the foliage, among the showiest of the native Gulf Coast butterworts. It grows abundantly in wet pine flatwoods and savannas from the Carolinas to Louisiana and is considered one of the easiest butterworts to cultivate, tolerating a broader range of moisture and light than many carnivorous plants as long as the soil stays consistently acidic and nutrient-poor. Grow in pure rain water or distilled water in the tray method and never fertilize; combine with sundews and pitcher plants for an authentic, low-maintenance Gulf Coast bog garden display.
sources: Carnivorous Plants of the Southeast (Larry Mellichamp)

planting.note: Plant only nursery-propagated leaf cuttings or divisions in spring in wet, acidic, nutrient-poor peat or sand in full sun to partial shade; Godfrey's butterwort is a federally threatened species restricted to a few counties in the Florida panhandle, and wild collection is illegal.

directions: Plant only nursery-propagated leaf cuttings or divisions in wet, acidic, nutrient-poor peat or sand in full sun to partial shade. Godfrey's butterwort is a federally threatened carnivorous plant known only from a handful of wet flatwoods and seepage bog sites in the Florida panhandle, closely related to blue butterwort but with pale violet flowers marked by a distinctive white-and-yellow throat, blooming in early spring above a low rosette of sticky, insect-trapping leaves. Because its entire wild range is so narrow and legally protected, it should be grown only from documented nursery propagation as a specialty addition to a Gulf Coast bog garden, never collected from the wild. Give it the same pure-water, no-fertilizer regimen required by all butterworts, and site it where consistent moisture and acidity can be reliably maintained year-round.
sources: US Fish and Wildlife Service — Species Profile

planting.note: Float a handful of stems in a sunny pond, water garden, or tub without soil; purple bladderwort has no roots and drifts or loosely anchors among other aquatic vegetation — use rain or pond water rather than chlorinated tap water.

directions: Place a clump of stems in a sunny, still or slow-moving acidic pond, water garden, or tub without adding soil; purple bladderwort floats free or drifts loosely among other aquatic plants and needs no planting medium at all. Its finely branched, whorled underwater stems carry small bladder traps, though unlike most bladderworts it is thought to rely on them more for anchorage and some prey capture than as its primary feeding strategy, since it also photosynthesizes readily in the nutrient-poor, tannin-stained waters it favors. From summer through early fall it produces small but vivid purple, orchid-like flowers held just above the water surface on slender stalks, among the most ornamental of the native bladderworts. It spreads readily in warm, acidic, still water across much of the eastern and southeastern US and is easily thinned by hand if it becomes too vigorous in a small water garden.

planting.note: Float a rosette in a sunny pond or water garden without soil; swollen bladderwort forms its own free-floating raft of spongy, inflated spokes and needs no anchoring — use rain or pond water rather than chlorinated tap water, and site it only in a contained water feature within its native Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain range.

directions: Float a rosette in a sunny, still, acidic pond or water garden without adding soil; swollen bladderwort is unmistakable among native bladderworts for the spoked, inflated float it produces where its finely divided, bladder-covered stems meet the water surface, buoying up a central cluster of showy, bright-yellow, snapdragon-like flowers held several inches above the water in summer. It is native to quiet, acidic, tannin-stained ponds and ditches across the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain, where its submerged stems trap tiny aquatic invertebrates in bladder traps while the plant drifts freely with the wind. In a home water garden it adds an architectural floating element unlike any typical aquatic plant, though it spreads readily in favorable warm, nutrient-poor water and should be thinned periodically and kept within a contained feature rather than released into open waterways outside its native range.

planting.note: Plant only nursery-propagated transplants in spring in wet to saturated, acidic, nutrient-poor peat or sphagnum in full sun; green pitcher plant is a federally endangered species restricted to a small number of mountain seepage bogs in northeast Alabama and adjacent Georgia and North Carolina, and wild collection is illegal.

directions: Plant only nursery-propagated transplants in wet to saturated, acidic, nutrient-poor peat or sphagnum in full sun. Green pitcher plant is a federally endangered species of upland seepage bogs and streamsides in the mountains and foothills of northeast Alabama and adjacent Georgia and North Carolina, growing at higher elevations and often in more shaded, cooler conditions than most Sarracenia. Its slender, yellow-green pitchers lack the strong red veining of many pitcher plants, and it blooms very early in spring, sometimes before the last frost, with nodding, pale yellow-green flowers on tall stalks that emerge before the season's pitchers fully unfurl. Because the species survives in only a handful of small, closely monitored wild populations, plant only stock propagated by reputable specialty carnivorous plant nurseries, and give it the same pure-water, nutrient-poor, sunny bog conditions required by all pitcher plants, with a cooler root zone than Gulf Coast species typically need.
sources: US Fish and Wildlife Service — Species Profile
